builder_plan.scenario: An agent looks good in demos, but you cannot tell which product tasks it fails.
builder_plan.change: Use the study's evaluation idea to inspect a small set of tasks with human-checked answers.
builder_plan.baseline: Your current evaluator and a manually reviewed reference set.
steps: Locate the paper's implementation and check its license, model support, data needs, and hardware requirements. Stop here if you cannot obtain the required artifacts.
Save a small set of representative product tasks and expected outcomes. Keep evaluation tasks out of any training or tuning, and choose quality and cost limits before running.
Run the baseline and the proposed change on identical inputs. Keep other settings fixed and repeat paired runs to expose variation.
Save per-task outputs, failures, timings, and all usage costs. Review regressions before expanding the test.
builder_plan.measure: Agreement with human review, missed failures, false alarms, and evaluation cost per task.
builder_plan.decision: Keep the change only if it meets your preselected quality and latency limits and improves the metric you care about after setup and operating costs. Otherwise retain the baseline. This is an exploration plan, not a validated recommendation.

title: WEAVE: Weaving Real-World Code Evolution into Dependency-Structured Tasks for Benchmarking and Training Code Agents
summary: WEAVE replaces single-PR, flat-scored repository benchmarks with DAGs of related PRs instantiated as unified executable tasks, plus a deterministic Graph Credit metric for dependency-consistent partial progress usable as RL reward. The cost is substantial: constructing verified multi-PR task graphs from real repositories, maintaining executable test environments per task, and running the SFT/RL training loop the framework is designed for, all of which exceed a single 24 GB GPU and a small cloud budget. It can fail through task-construction errors (misidentified change loci or broken dependency edges), tests that do not fully capture intended behavior so Graph Credit rewards the wrong progress, and limited transfer if the reader's target repositories differ from the curated PR histories.
rationale: The method addresses benchmarking and training of code agents rather than improving an existing production inference stack, and its construction and RL training requirements exceed the reader's constrained infrastructure, so it merits monitoring rather than adoption.
technique: Dependency-structured multi-PR code tasks with test-grounded partial credit
